memory_update.text: PLPC is a rare listed pure-ish public play on transmission hardware plus robotic installation systems; it belongs in the underfollowed lane for grid labor/automation research.
MYRG is a smaller specialty contractor with direct T&D exposure and explicit utility line installation activity, making it a useful labor-constrained grid-build proxy.
For this node, the investable surface is split between hardware that reduces installation time and contractors whose throughput is constrained by craft labor availability.
The market appears to pay more attention to large contractors and diversified industrials than to transmission hardware vendors that can improve installation productivity.

PLPC is the highest-priority underfollowed candidate for the grid construction labor and installation automation node because it combines transmission-line hardware exposure with disclosed robotic installation partnerships.

CTOS should be tracked as a specialty utility fleet-capacity enabler; its exposure is less glamorous but directly tied to bucket trucks, digger derricks, cranes, stringing gear, parts, and utility contractor deployment speed.
TEX is a broader industrial name with a utility-equipment wedge; keep it in the universe but require segment-level materiality before promoting it beyond Layer 1.
BLS data supports that lineworker work is skilled, hazardous, equipment-intensive, and projected to grow faster than average from 2024 to 2034, supporting the labor-capacity framing.
Several highly relevant private companies appear in this node, including FulcrumAir, Altec, LineWise, and MacLean Power Systems; public-market mapping may therefore be indirect and requires caution.

PLPC should be promoted as the highest-priority underfollowed candidate for this node because official evidence links its overhead-line hardware to robotic installation systems, directly matching the labor-productivity bottleneck hypothesis.

CTOS is a second-order grid labor/productivity enabler through specialty utility equipment rental and fleet access, especially if contractors face bottlenecks in aerial devices, digger derricks, stringing gear, and related tools.

TEX is a diversified equipment name with a potentially underappreciated Terex Utilities exposure; verify whether utility bucket-truck and digger-derrick capacity is material enough for consolidated results.

For this node, reference contractors such as MYRG validate the labor bottleneck, while alpha-hunt candidates should emphasize hardware, tools, fleet access, robotics, safety systems, and installation data capture that let scarce crews do more work.

Private companies appear important in the true chokepoint map: FulcrumAir, Altec, MacLean Power Systems, Sherman+Reilly, and several robotic inspection/installation vendors may control key products but are not clean public-market exposures.

PLPC should be prioritized for later Serenity layers as the cleanest underfollowed public mapping to robotic/low-labor overhead-line hardware installation, but commercialization and revenue materiality are still unproven.
TEX is a second-order utility-construction productivity candidate because Terex Utilities equipment is used in overhead electric-line construction and maintenance; purity is lower than PLPC.
MYRG is a useful labor-bottleneck reference signal: rising backlog plus commentary on qualified personnel, wage inflation, or project timing would support the broader node thesis.

Need deeper search for public providers of lineworker training, inspection drones, utility field-service software, safety systems, and specialized distributors; this pass found stronger evidence for hardware/equipment than for software or training providers.

node: Grid construction labor, lineworker availability, and installation automation
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Direct public exposure here clusters around transmission/distribution hardware suppliers and specialty contractors that either reduce installation labor per mile or depend on scarce craft labor to complete grid builds. The most direct underfollowed names are PLPC and MYRG; HUBB and PWR serve as higher-attention reference anchors. This pass expands the universe around the hypothesis that grid buildout may be constrained by skilled lineworker availability and field productivity, not only by electrical equipment supply. The strongest underfollowed candidates are companies supplying transmission-line hardware compatible with robotic installation, specialty utility fleet equipment, and rental/sales infrastructure that lets utilities and contractors scale crews faster. Obvious contractor exposure is included only as a reference lane. Layer 1B expansion found one unusually direct underfollowed automation/hardware candidate, PLPC, plus adjacent productivity enablers in specialty utility equipment rental, bucket/digger-derrick manufacturing, and specialty electrical construction labor capacity. The strongest node fit is PLPC because official company evidence confirms robotic installation systems designed around PLP overhead-line hardware. CTOS and TEX are second-order capacity enablers: they do not solve the lineworker shortage directly, but they supply or rent the specialized equipment that lets scarce crews work. MYRG is a reference/direct labor-capacity name rather than an obscure automation beneficiary, useful as a demand and capacity context anchor. No buy/sell recommendation i
